title: Separate worlds of misinformation. An explorative study of checked claims in German public broadcast news and talk shows
screen_reason: Semi-automated matching of 462 claims checked by six German fact-checking organisations against the subtitles of 1,382 episodes of ten German public broadcast news and political talk shows (June 2023 to June 2024). Reports the share of episodes containing at least one fact-checked false claim, overall (4.85%) and separately for talk shows (11.62%) and news shows (2.28%). These are content shares with an item denominator: CONTENT.

estimates.platform: German public broadcast television (news and political talk shows)
estimates.measure_type: % of public broadcast TV episodes containing at least one statement matching a fact-checked false claim
estimates.value_raw: 77 matches in 67 episodes, 4.85% of the 1382 episodes
estimates.denominator: 1,382 episodes of four public broadcast news programmes and six political talk shows aired between June 2023 and June 2024
estimates.definition: The episode's subtitles contained a statement judged semantically identical to a claim that a German fact-checking organisation had checked and found false, misleading, exaggerated or unfounded
estimates.misinfo_def: "the term ‘misinformation’ is used to denote inaccurate claims, regardless of intent to deceive and the type of deception"
estimates.source_quote: It finds 77 matches in 67 episodes, amounting to 4.85% of the 1382 episodes during the sampling period between June 2023 and June 2024.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Claims checked by six German fact-checking organisations (AFP, Correctiv, dpa, ARD Faktenfinder, BR Faktenfuchs, Hart aber Fair Faktencheck); candidate matches retrieved with an e5 embedding model, filtered by ChatGPT few-shot classification (F1 84.21%), then validated by three student annotators (75% agreement on the double-coded subset) and finally reviewed by the author against the full fact-check and the video. Estimated false negative rate of the retrieval pipeline: 14%.
estimates.moderator_quote: This study employed two data sources: subtitles from ten German public broadcast news or talk shows between June 2023 and June 2024 (n = 1382) and checked claims in articles from six German fact-checking organizations between January 2023 and June 2024 (n = 462).
estimates.notes: This is a lower bound by construction: only claims that a German fact-checker had already checked could be matched, and the author calls the study exploratory rather than representative. The unit is the episode, not the claim, so the value is the share of programmes touched by checked misinformation. Ten shows were purposively chosen as the most watched in their categories (denom_selection curated), but all their episodes in the window were searched (full_census). Year set to the end of the window (June 2023 to June 2024).

estimates.ground_truth_detail: As above: fact-check corpus matched semi-automatically, human-validated.
estimates.moderator_quote: Overall, talk shows demon strated a greater propensity (14.79%, or 11.62% without Hart aber Fair matches with itself) for matches than news shows (2.28%).

The moderator_quote reproduces a line the PDF hyphenates across a line break ('demon-strated').

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the per-show match rates in Table 4 (Hart aber Fair 35.48%, Maischberger 24.07%, Markus Lanz 9.77%, Maybrit Illner 10.53%, Anne Will 7.14%, Heute Journal 3.21%, Tagesthemen 2.44%, Tagesschau 2.13%, Heute 1.38%, Caren Miosga 0%) - single-programme breakdowns below the format level, with small denominators; (b) the deception-type split of the matched claims (32% entirely false, 31% unfounded, 22% misleading) - this is falsity computed inside a misinformation-only sample (R3, within_misinfo_content) and the text does not say whether the denominator is the 77 matches or the 29 unique claims, so it is not codeable with confidence; (c) the reaction split (53% contradicted, 40% uncommented, 6% agreed) and the topic split (31% institutional bias, 27% pull factors, 12% migration, 9% climate, 4% benefits), which describe the misinformation set, not prevalence; (d) Table 5's match rates by fact-checking organisation (overall 4.98%; Hart aber Fair 31.58%, Faktenfinder 26.09%, Faktenfuchs 22.22%, AFP 2.13%, Correctiv 1.85%, dpa 0.84%) - the denominator is fact-checks, so this measures the method's yield, not misinformation on television; (e) the share of AfD talk show appearances featuring a checked claim (about 35%) and comparable party figures, which are speaker-level subgroups; (f) the platform origin of the checked claims (Facebook 33%, Twitter 11%, TikTok 9%, public broadcasting 18%, t-online 15%; 57% from social media or messengers), which describes where the claims came from. Worth a human's attention: the authors state plainly that the sample cannot support a representative prevalence estimate, because only already-fact-checked claims can be matched and German fact-checkers mostly check anonymous online claims. The 4.85% should be read as a floor, not a prevalence.

rob.design: Census of 1,382 episodes of the ten most-watched German public broadcast news and political talk shows (June 2023 to June 2024, subtitles) matched against 462 claims checked by six German fact-checking organisations (January 2023 to June 2024). Pipeline: 140,393,022 claim-subtitle pairs reduced by e5 vector search to 317,096, by ChatGPT few-shot classification to 1,384, validated by three student annotators to 403 (two annotators on the 235 Hart aber Fair pairs, 75% agreement; single annotator elsewhere), de-overlapped by the author to 210, and reduced to 77 confirmed matches after the author watched each scene. Estimated false negative rate 14%. Discursive coding of the 77 matches was done by a single expert coder, with no inter-coder reliability, which the author justifies and flags. Main threat: the fact-check corpus is a non-representative selection, so the prevalence is a lower bound.
